new_statements.rule_in_words: The author treats stress and vowel length together and says they fall on the penultimate syllable; but the same paragraph presents length as lexically contrastive (seven minimal pairs differing only in penult length, e.g. 'smell' vs 'nose'), he elsewhere notes final stress on the self-name Dumaget, and Reid's 1991 phonetic wordlists mark many Southern Alta words with a final accent and others with a long penult. The most natural reconciliation is the common Philippine pattern (long/stressed penult vs. final stress, lexically determined), which is how Wikipedia summarises Abreu ('phonemic, but unpredictable'), but Abreu's own sentence literally says penultimate. Hence provisional reading unclear or contradictory; if forced, lexical penult-vs-final contrast realised as penult length.
new_statements.exceptions: Endonym Dumaget 'with stress on the final syllable' (attributed to an East-Luzon Negrito areal vowel change, after Reid 2013); plural formation by penult vowel lengthening (Table 8.7, p. 293: Ɂanak 'child' -> /Ɂa.nak/ 'children'); loan clusters/affricates excluded from native inventory. No IPA stress marks are used anywhere in the grammar, only ':' for length.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level citation forms in phonemic transcription; no discussion of phrase-level prominence or of stress shift under affixation. Grammar is based on the Kabuloan variety of Southern Alta spoken in Bulacan/Nueva Ecija (DLSU fieldwork 2014-2018).
new_statements.identity_note: Abreu 2018 describes the Kabuloan (Kabulowan/Kabuloan Dumagat) variety of Southern Alta (agy, sout2905) as spoken around Bulacan and Nueva Ecija; Reid 1991 notes a phonologically more conservative dialect ('Edimala') at Dicapanikian/Dicapanisan on the Aurora coast which neither source describes prosodically. Not to be confused with Northern Alta (nort2875) or Umiray Dumaget (umir1236).

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Southern Alta has an empty rule; the existing statement (Abreu 2018, p. 98) says 'Stress or vowel length of the words always fall on the penultimate syllable' and is read as unclear. The 2014 abstract's marks agree with penult in 4 of 6 marked words but two marked words (antepenult 'green', initial 'tall') are incompatible with 'always penultimate'. Weak evidence: no rule text, most words unmarked, the transcription is impressionistic (mixed /ɐ/ vs /a/, 'nohw', 'beeyah'). It does not support entering a fixed: penultimate syllable rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule is stated. The abstract says only that stress is 'shown in the sample words', and primary-stress marks appear on 6 of roughly 30 sample words: 4 on the penult (/ˈa.pun/, /ˈmot.nohw/, /u.ˈma.beeyah/, /mɐ.ˈa.boŋ/) and 2 earlier (/ˈnɐ.li.nahw/ antepenult; /ˈmo.dʒɪ.ŋɐ.tŏ/ initial, fourth from the end). The remaining words carry no mark at all, so the marking is unsystematic and does not establish any placement.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The two non-penult marks (/ˈnɐ.li.nahw/ 'green', /ˈmo.dʒɪ.ŋɐ.tŏ/ 'tall') are the only data bearing on exceptions to a penult rule.
new_statements.identity_note: The 2014 abstract describes 'Kailugan Dumaget', the speech of one Bulacan community (a native couple, their kin and neighbours in Bulacan, Sierra Madre), i.e. the Bulacan (Kabuloan/Kabulowan) variety of Southern Alta [agy] that Abreu later described in the 2018 grammar as Kabuloan Dumagat; the abstract itself says its description 'is only of one kind' of Southern Alta and repeats a Joshua Project claim that Southern Alta 'has six different languages' (a people-profile claim, not a linguistic one). Same language as the catalog entry, one local variety.

readall_conflicts: Abreu 2018 (the reference grammar, p. 98) says 'Stress or vowel length of the words always fall on the penultimate syllable', but the sentence conflates stress with contrastive penult vowel length (its minimal pairs /Ɂa.ŋƆt/ 'smell' vs /Ɂa.ŋƆt/ 'nose' etc. show length, not stress, as the contrast), and the same grammar (p. 46, extracted text) quotes Himmelmann that in Philippine languages 'stress placement is not predictable and may occur on either the penultimate or the ultimate syllable'. The English Wikipedia article, citing Abreu 2018, summarises the language as 'Stress is phonemic, but unpredictable' and 'Vowels are lengthened when in a stressed syllable', which is the opposite of a fixed: penultimate syllable reading. The 2014 abstract by the same author gives no rule and marks primary stress on the penult in four words but on the antepenult in nalinaw 'green' and on the initial (fourth-from-last) syllable in modyingato 'tall'. Reid 1991 (already held by the project) has no stress statement and only phonetic length and acute marks in wordlists. Net: the only explicit rule sentence (2018, always penult) is contradicted by the author's own 2014 stress marks and by the Wikipedia reading of the same grammar; nothing here is solid enough to replace the catalog's empty rule with a fixed placement.

sources.note: Historical-comparative paper (reflexes of *R, *j, *k, *ə, gemination); no statement on stress. Fn. 11: 'A careful phonemic analysis has not been completed.. All transcriptions are phonetic'. The Southern Alta wordlists (Table 1 etc.) transcribe both penultimate length (ʔa:ŋut 'nose', ba:kal 'bolo', pa:saʔ 'boil') and final acute accents (ʔilóm 'ant', sulá 'anus', malawák 'butterfly', ʔusáŋ 'charcoal', lawáy 'seek', kalád 'different', layát 'wide'), i.e. data consistent with a penult-vs-final contrast, but no rule is stated.
